sentences.text: The skull of Dentaneosuchus stood taller than it was wide, a shape known as altirostral.
Its upper jaw featured five teeth on each side of the premaxilla, with the fourth tooth being twice as large as the second.
The nasal bone was long, extending from the front of the snout to the frontal bone, and it was fused with the maxilla.
This animal is recognized as the largest land-based predator ever found in Cenozoic Europe.
Four bony armor plates were found, including a larger sub-trapezoid shape and a smaller, wider-than-long oval type.
The first remains were unearthed in the Sables du Castrais Formation near Issel, France, and originally named Atacisaurus crassiproratus by Gaston Astre in 1931.
In 2018, Godinot and colleagues reclassified this species as Iberosuchus crassiproratus.
Martin and colleagues formally described the genus Dentaneosuchus in 2023, establishing Dentaneosuchus crassiproratus as the type species.
Currently, only two recorded fossil occurrences of this animal exist.
As an apex predator, it was capable of hunting large prey, though the exact species it targeted remain unknown.
Its massive size suggests it could prey on animals of its own size or larger, such as the early perissodactyl Lophiodon lautricense, which weighed up to 2,000 kg.
This creature exhibited massive dimensions, matching the trend of increasing size seen in contemporary European mammal species.
Dentaneosuchus belongs to the class Reptilia and the parent group Sebecoidea.
Phylogenetic analysis places it in the family Sebecidae, closely related to the South American Baurusuchidae within the group Sebecosuchia.
Within Sebecidae, the animal was recovered as having affinities with the German genus Bergisuchus.
Fossils have been found in Issel and Réalmont in France, with the range currently confined to the Bartonian stage of the Eocene.

Some localities previously associated with Dentaneosuchus were placed in the MP13-14 biozones (Lutetian), an age similar to the Spanish Duero Basin and much older than the Réalmont locality in France.
The presence of sebecids in Europe, far from their primary range in South America, remains not entirely resolved.
The origins of European sebecids are a debated subject due to a poor fossil record outside of South America.
A major issue with the North American dispersal hypothesis is the complete absence of sebecid material in continental North America, with only a ziphodont tooth from Cuba as potential evidence.
It is debated why crocodylomorphs lost their position as top predators in Europe by the end of the Eocene.
Researchers suggest that differences between Dentaneosuchus and Bergisuchus might change with age, but conclude it is premature to make conclusive statements on the implications.
Authors note that many unknowns regarding Dentaneosuchus anatomy could greatly impact its phylogenetic placement and that future discoveries could change its position drastically.
